screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we move from requirements to the surface clients use every day: the A P I. A clear A P I defines how users create, retrieve, and manage resources. You'll learn concrete endpoints for two small services — a URL Shortener and a Pastebin — with example request/response bodies, common error responses, and the reasoning behind choices like status codes and redirect types. Throughout, concrete examples and a short Flask starter will show how these rules map to code. By the end you will be able to design endpoint contracts that are easy for clients to use, simple to document, and robust enough to evolve. Think about how your consumers will retry, read errors, and discover the A P I — that perspective guides many design choices.

screens.title: Bloom's Progression
screens.narratorSegment: This progression shows how you'll move from understanding to mastery. First, you will learn the canonical HTTP methods and when to use them. Next, you'll understand request and response shapes, status codes, and how redirects differ in practice. Then you'll apply these ideas by drafting endpoints for both the shortener and the paste service and testing simple client/server exchanges. Finally, you'll aim to master production concerns: making operations idempotent where needed, adding versioning so you don't break clients, and putting in basic rate limits and authentication. Each stage pairs a concrete task with the reason it matters: safety, observability, and long-term compatibility. For example, choosing 302 instead of 301 lets you keep analytics and change targets; that flexibility is a deliberate design trade-off. This flow gives you both practical templates and judgment criteria so you can design APIs that are easy to evolve while being safe for clients to rely on.

screens.title: RESTful API fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: RESTful is an architectural style that guides how we use HTTP as the surface for services. In practice this means mapping resources to URLs, using HTTP verbs semantically, and keeping each request self-contained so servers do not rely on shared session state. For example, when you design a paste resource you treat each paste as an entity with its own URL like /api/v1/pastes/{pasteId}. A POST to /api/v1/pastes creates a new paste and returns a 201 Created with metadata. A GET to that same resource returns the content and a 200 OK. Statelessness means the server should not expect previous interactions to carry state; any authorization, pagination, or context must be included in the request. This reduces server-side complexity and improves scalability. A common misconception is treating REST as a strict checklist — it's a set of guiding principles. Using HTTP effectively also improves client behavior: predictable methods allow safe retries, status codes convey results without reading body content, and consistent resource naming reduces confusion. Always document required fields and expected errors so clients can react deterministically. For practice, think of a paste resource and name the verbs and responses you would expect; that clarity drives robust integrations.

keyIdea.title: Stateless resources
keyIdea.text: Map entities to URLs and use HTTP verbs and status codes so clients can interact predictably.

content.html:
Core Concept
RESTful API fundamentals
Resources, verbs, and stateless communication
Definition & rules
  • Resources as URLs: Each entity gets its own stable path, e.g., /api/v1/pastes/{pasteId}.
  • HTTP verbs: GET for read, POST for create, PUT/PATCH for update, DELETE for removal.
  • Stateless: Requests carry all context needed, including auth and pagination tokens.
  • Consistent names: Use predictable naming and casing for fields to avoid client confusion.
Analogy
Think of the API as a well-labeled library: each book (resource) has a shelf address (URL) and a clear borrowing rule (verb).
Concrete example: Paste resource
{
  "pasteId": "xyzAbC12",
  "content": "console.log('Hello, Cohortia!');",
  "syntaxHighlightingLanguage": "javascript",
  "accessControl": "public",
  "createdAt": "2024-07-20T10:30:00Z"
}
Clients expect consistent fields and status codes when creating or retrieving this resource.
Key Takeaway
Design resources and verbs so clients can rely on method semantics and status codes instead of brittle behavior.

screens.title: URL Shortener — POST /api/v1/shorten
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a short URL is a straightforward create operation. The recommended pattern is POST /api/v1/shorten with a JSON body that includes the original longUrl and optional fields such as customShortCode and expirationDate. The server must validate the longUrl format and check customShortCode availability if supplied. On success, return 201 Created with the generated shortUrl, shortCode, and metadata like createdAt and expirationDate. On client errors — invalid URL format or a taken custom code — return 400 Bad Request with a clear error and details. This contract keeps the client flow simple: submit a URL, receive a short code and full short URL. One practical point: make the shortCode part of the response so clients can show or copy it directly. Another consideration is idempotence: POST is normally non-idempotent; if you need idempotent create operations, consider accepting a client-generated idempotency key or switch to PUT semantics on a deterministic resource path. For analytics and debugging include timestamps and the shortCode in responses. A clear example request and success response are provided visually so you can copy them into client code. URL Shortener — POST /api/v1/shorten means post /api/v1/shorten creates a new short url and should validate input and return 201 created with the short code.. In practical terms, create short links with optional custom code and expiration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Endpoint Design
URL Shortener — POST /api/v1/shorten
Creation contract, validation rules, and sample responses
Request Body (JSON)
{
  "longUrl": "https://www.example.com/this/is/a/very/long/url?param=1",
  "customShortCode": "my-awesome-link",
  "expirationDate": "2024-12-31T23:59:59Z"
}
longUrl is required. Validate format and uniqueness of customShortCode on the server.
Success Response (201 Created)
{
  "shortUrl": "https://cohortia.ly/aBcDeFg",
  "longUrl": "https://www.example.com/...",
  "shortCode": "aBcDeFg",
  "expirationDate": "2024-12-31T23:59:59Z",
  "createdAt": "2024-07-20T10:30:00Z"
}
Include the shortCode so clients can copy or display it without parsing the URL.
Error Example
400 Bad Request: return an object with an error and details field so clients can show actionable messages.
Key Takeaway

Use POST for create, validate input, and return 201 with the short code and metadata.

Pro Tip

If you need idempotency on create, accept an idempotency key or consider deterministic PUT based on a client-supplied resource id.

screens.title: Redirecting — GET /{shortCode}
screens.narratorSegment: Redirects are retrievals with a special delivery: instead of returning a resource body, the server sends a redirect status and a Location header pointing to the long URL. Typically a dedicated redirect service handles GET /{shortCode} so it can be optimized for low latency. You must choose between 301 Moved Permanently and 302 Found (or 307 Temporary Redirect). A 301 signals permanence and is often cached by browsers and proxies, which reduces server load but prevents later changes to the mapping — this can harm analytics and updates. A 302 avoids caching so every click reaches your service, enabling click tracking and dynamic behavior like geo-routing or A/B tests. For public shorteners, 302 is commonly preferred for flexibility. Always return 404 Not Found if the code does not exist or has expired. Include appropriate cache-control headers when you want proxies to respect your choice. A frequent misconception is thinking redirect type only affects SEO; it also defines caching and client behavior. Choose based on whether mappings remain stable and whether each hit should be visible to your analytics pipeline. Redirecting — GET /{shortCode} means 302 is flexible and analytics-friendly; 301 caches and is permanent. choose based on changeability and performance needs.. In practical terms, redirect responses, caching, and analytics trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow
Redirecting — GET /{shortCode}
How the redirect service responds and why code choice matters
Behavior
  • Receive GET /{shortCode} and look up the mapping.
  • If found and active, return redirect with Location header to long URL.
  • If not found or expired, return 404 Not Found.
A dedicated redirect service improves throughput and latency for high-volume click traffic.
Redirect types
301 Moved Permanently
Cached by browsers; good for permanent mappings; limits updates.
302 Found / 307 Temporary
Not cached; allows analytics and later updates.
Choose 302 when you need every click to hit your servers for tracking or dynamic logic.
Example Response
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: https://www.example.com/this/is/a/very/long/url
Key Takeaway
Redirect type affects caching and analytics. Prefer 302 for flexibility, 301 when mapping is permanent.
Common Mistake
Using 301 by default then expecting to update mappings later — browser caches can make updates invisible.

screens.title: Pastebin — POST /api/v1/pastes
screens.narratorSegment: A Pastebin create flow is another create operation: POST /api/v1/pastes. The request must include content and may include optional fields such as syntaxHighlightingLanguage, expirationOption, accessControl, and a password for private pastes. The server validates content length and required fields and derives expirationDate from the chosen expirationOption. On success return 201 Created with pasteUrl and pasteId plus metadata like createdAt and expirationDate. If required fields are missing return 400 Bad Request with clear details, and if a password is required but not supplied return a 400 error describing the issue. For private pastes, the retrieve flow should require an authorization or a separate unlock step that accepts a password. One misconception is returning full error stacks or internal debugging information in error bodies — avoid exposing internals. Design responses so clients can render a link immediately and know when a paste expires. This contract supports features like unlisted vs public pastes and lays the groundwork for access checks during retrieval. screens.title: Paste Retrieve — GET and Unlock
screens.narratorSegment: Retrieval has two patterns for a Pastebin: direct GET for public/unlisted pastes and a separate unlock step for password-protected ones. For public pastes a GET /api/v1/pastes/{pasteId} returns 200 OK with the paste content and metadata. If the paste is not found or expired return 404 Not Found. For private pastes, require the client to authenticate or to POST a password to /api/v1/pastes/{pasteId}/unlock. On successful unlock return the paste content and an otherwise appropriate 200 OK. If the password is missing or incorrect return 403 Forbidden to indicate an authorization problem. Design the unlock endpoint to avoid leaking information; for instance, do not reveal whether a paste exists in error messages. A common mistake is using the same response code for missing paste and wrong password; instead use 404 for non-existent, 403 for authorization failure. Also plan for authorization headers or A P I tokens for user-scoped pastes. This clear separation of retrieval and unlocking keeps public reads fast while isolating authentication checks to a narrower flow. Paste Retrieve — GET and Unlock means use get for public retrieval and a dedicated unlock endpoint for private, password-protected pastes to keep flows explicit.. In practical terms, retrieving public pastes and unlocking private ones. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: 301 vs 302 and caching implications
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between 301 and 302 affects more than SEO: it controls client and proxy caching. A 301 Moved Permanently is often cached by browsers and intermediaries, which can bypass your redirect service on subsequent requests. That helps performance but makes changing the target URL difficult because clients may never re-query the shortener. A 302 Found or 307 Temporary Redirect avoids that caching behavior so every click hits your service. That is useful when you want to gather analytics on each click, perform per-request logic, or update mappings. If you need analytics, URL editing, or A/B testing, prefer 302. If mapping is truly permanent and you want to offload traffic from your servers, 301 is acceptable. Remember to include Cache-Control headers when you need finer control. A common misconception is that 301 is always better for SEO; while often true, SEO must be balanced against operational needs like analytics. The decision should align with product goals: flexibility and measurement versus long-term permanence and reduced server load. 301 vs 302 and caching implications means use 302 for flexibility and analytics; use 301 when mappings are permanent and you want caching benefits.. In practical terms, how redirect type affects caching, analytics, and updateability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Comparison
301 vs 302 and caching implications
Balance permanence and analytics needs
301 Moved Permanently
  • Browsers and proxies often cache the redirect.
  • Reduces server load but makes updates difficult.

302 Found / 307 Temporary Redirect
  • Not cached; every request hits your service.
  • Enables analytics, dynamic routing, and updates to targets.

Practical rule

Hands-on
Flask starter: POST /api/v1/shorten
Run locally to test validation and basic responses
Starter code (save as app.py)
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify
import uuid

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route('/api/v1/shorten', methods=['POST'])
def shorten_url():
  data = request.get_json()
  if not data or 'longUrl' not in data:
    return jsonify({"error": "Missing 'longUrl' in request body"}), 400

  long_url = data['longUrl']
  if not (long_url.startswith('http://') or long_url.startswith('https://')):
    return jsonify({"error": "Invalid URL format", "details": "URL must start with http:// or https://"}), 400

  short_code = str(uuid.uuid4())[:7]
  short_url = f"https://cohortia.ly/{short_code}"

  response = {
    "shortUrl": short_url,
    "longUrl": long_url,
    "shortCode": short_code,
    "createdAt": "2024-07-20T10:30:00Z"
  }
  return jsonify(response), 201

if __name__ == '__main__':
  app.run(debug=True, port=5000)

screens.title: Idempotence and safe retries
screens.narratorSegment: Idempotence is crucial for resilient APIs because network clients may retry requests automatically. An idempotent operation produces the same result whether it is applied once or multiple times. In HTTP, GET, PUT, and DELETE are expected to be idempotent; POST is not. For example, deleting a resource twice with DELETE yields the same final state as deleting it once. Creating a new resource with POST typically creates duplicates if retried, which can be problematic. To handle this, APIs can accept idempotency keys supplied by clients; the server stores the key and ensures the operation only executes once for that key. Alternatively, use deterministic PUT on a resource path derived from a client-provided id so repeated calls replace the same resource. A misconception is thinking that POST cannot ever be safe to retry — with an idempotency key or a unique client-generated identifier, POST can be made effectively idempotent. Always document which operations are safe to retry, and consider returning idempotency results and guidance in error messages so clients can react appropriately. Idempotence and safe retries means use idempotency keys or deterministic resource ids to allow safe retries for operations that would otherwise duplicate work.. In practical terms, when repeated requests should not cause duplicate effects. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Core Concept
Idempotence and safe retries
Design patterns that prevent duplicate effects
Definition
An operation is idempotent if applying it multiple times has the same effect as applying it once.
Patterns
  • Idempotency keys: store keys server-side to deduplicate requests.
  • Deterministic PUT: client chooses resource id so repeated calls overwrite the same resource.
  • Use PUT/DELETE for operations expected to be safely retried; document POST behavior.
Concrete example
If a client POSTs to create a short URL and the client times out, they may retry. Without idempotency this can produce multiple short codes. Provide an idempotency-key header and store the result linked to that key so retries return the same short URL.
Misconception
POST is always unsafe. With idempotency or deterministic resource IDs you can make creates safe to retry.

screens.title: Security, rate limiting, and versioning
screens.narratorSegment: APIs must be protected and evolvable. Start with authentication: for user-scoped or management actions require A P I keys or OAuth tokens so actions like creating custom short codes or private pastes are attributed and revocable. For public create endpoints you may allow anonymous usage but apply stricter rate limits. Rate limiting prevents abuse and ensures fairness; return headers like X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, and X-RateLimit-Reset so clients can back off gracefully. Input validation is a security first step: validate URL formats, enforce maximum content lengths for pastes, and sanitize fields before persisting. Avoid returning internal stack traces in error bodies. Versioning is essential: include /v1/ in your paths so you can introduce breaking changes in /v2/ without breaking existing clients. Common mistakes include not versioning, inconsistent naming conventions, and exposing internal identifiers in error messages. Start with conservative defaults: require auth for user-sensitive flows, apply modest rate limits to anonymous endpoints, and scope version changes carefully. These controls give you breathing room to iterate without harming existing integrations. Operational Concerns
Security, rate limiting, and versioning
Basic protections and evolution strategies
Authentication
Use API keys or tokens for actions tied to users. Keep public endpoints limited and monitor for abuse.
Rate limiting
Throttle clients and return headers like X-RateLimit-Limit and X-RateLimit-Remaining so clients can adapt.
Versioning
Include /v1/ in paths. When breaking changes arrive, publish /v2/ rather than changing existing contracts.

  • Not versioning APIs and then breaking clients.

  • Failing to validate inputs and allowing oversized payloads or malformed URLs.

screens.title: Common API design mistakes & checklist
screens.narratorSegment: This checklist captures practical mistakes I see often and the corrective design choices to prevent them. First, avoid using inappropriate HTTP methods — creation should use POST, retrieval GET, updates PUT/PATCH, and deletion DELETE. Second, return clear error responses with appropriate status codes like 400 for validation errors, 403 for authorization failures, 404 for missing resources, and 500 only for server faults. Third, version your A P I paths so breaking changes can coexist with older clients. Fourth, validate all inputs to prevent malformed data and security issues, and do not expose internal debug data. Fifth, apply rate limiting and return informative headers so clients can back off gracefully. Sixth, think about idempotence for retry safety and include idempotency keys where useful. Use consistent naming and JSON field casing across endpoints. Following this checklist reduces integration friction, simplifies client code, and keeps your service manageable as traffic grows. Common API design mistakes & checklist
Short list to validate before launch

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we move from requirements to the surface clients use every day: the A P I. A clear A P I defines how users create, retrieve, and manage resources. We focus on RESTful principles: using HTTP methods semantically, staying stateless, and returning predictable JSON payloads and status codes. You'll learn concrete endpoints for two small services — a URL Shortener and a Pastebin — with example request/response bodies, common error responses, and the reasoning behind choices like status codes and redirect types. We will also cover safety checks that matter early: versioning to avoid breaking clients, input validation to prevent malformed data, idempotence to make retries safe, and basic rate limiting and authentication patterns to prevent abuse. Throughout, concrete examples and a short Flask starter will show how these rules map to code. By the end you will be able to design endpoint contracts that are easy for clients to use, simple to document, and robust enough to evolve. Think about how your consumers will retry, read errors, and discover the A P I — that perspective guides many design choices.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to define RESTful endpoints for two example services, write clear JSON request and response shapes, and choose appropriate HTTP status codes. First, you'll design create and redirect endpoints for a URL Shortener, including how to accept optional custom short codes and expiration dates. Second, you'll design create and retrieve endpoints for a Pastebin, including access control, expiration, and password-protected retrieval flows. Third, you'll explain idempotence and when safe methods matter, for example how retries can be made safe or unsafe depending on whether you use POST, PUT, or DELETE. Finally, you'll identify initial security measures: A P I keys or tokens, rate limiting headers, and input validation to stop malformed or malicious requests. Each objective pairs a practical task — writing an endpoint contract — with the reason it matters in production: reliability, observability, and client compatibility. You'll practice with a short Flask starter that shows a POST /shorten implementation, and you'll review common mistakes to avoid. These objectives focus on making APIs predictable, safe to evolve, and straightforward for clients to use.

This progression shows how you'll move from understanding to mastery. First, you will learn the canonical HTTP methods and when to use them. Next, you'll understand request and response shapes, status codes, and how redirects differ in practice. Then you'll apply these ideas by drafting endpoints for both the shortener and the paste service and testing simple client/server exchanges. Finally, you'll aim to master production concerns: making operations idempotent where needed, adding versioning so you don't break clients, and putting in basic rate limits and authentication. Each stage pairs a concrete task with the reason it matters: safety, observability, and long-term compatibility. For example, choosing 302 instead of 301 lets you keep analytics and change targets; that flexibility is a deliberate design trade-off. This flow gives you both practical templates and judgment criteria so you can design APIs that are easy to evolve while being safe for clients to rely on.

RESTful is an architectural style that guides how we use HTTP as the surface for services. In practice this means mapping resources to URLs, using HTTP verbs semantically, and keeping each request self-contained so servers do not rely on shared session state. For example, when you design a paste resource you treat each paste as an entity with its own URL like /api/v1/pastes/{pasteId}. A POST to /api/v1/pastes creates a new paste and returns a 201 Created with metadata. A GET to that same resource returns the content and a 200 OK. Statelessness means the server should not expect previous interactions to carry state; any authorization, pagination, or context must be included in the request. This reduces server-side complexity and improves scalability. A common misconception is treating REST as a strict checklist — it's a set of guiding principles. Using HTTP effectively also improves client behavior: predictable methods allow safe retries, status codes convey results without reading body content, and consistent resource naming reduces confusion. Always document required fields and expected errors so clients can react deterministically. For practice, think of a paste resource and name the verbs and responses you would expect; that clarity drives robust integrations.

Creating a short URL is a straightforward create operation. The recommended pattern is POST /api/v1/shorten with a JSON body that includes the original longUrl and optional fields such as customShortCode and expirationDate. The server must validate the longUrl format and check customShortCode availability if supplied. On success, return 201 Created with the generated shortUrl, shortCode, and metadata like createdAt and expirationDate. On client errors — invalid URL format or a taken custom code — return 400 Bad Request with a clear error and details. This contract keeps the client flow simple: submit a URL, receive a short code and full short URL. One practical point: make the shortCode part of the response so clients can show or copy it directly. Another consideration is idempotence: POST is normally non-idempotent; if you need idempotent create operations, consider accepting a client-generated idempotency key or switch to PUT semantics on a deterministic resource path. For analytics and debugging include timestamps and the shortCode in responses. A clear example request and success response are provided visually so you can copy them into client code. URL Shortener — POST /api/v1/shorten means post /api/v1/shorten creates a new short url and should validate input and return 201 created with the short code.. In practical terms, create short links with optional custom code and expiration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Redirects are retrievals with a special delivery: instead of returning a resource body, the server sends a redirect status and a Location header pointing to the long URL. Typically a dedicated redirect service handles GET /{shortCode} so it can be optimized for low latency. You must choose between 301 Moved Permanently and 302 Found (or 307 Temporary Redirect). A 301 signals permanence and is often cached by browsers and proxies, which reduces server load but prevents later changes to the mapping — this can harm analytics and updates. A 302 avoids caching so every click reaches your service, enabling click tracking and dynamic behavior like geo-routing or A/B tests. For public shorteners, 302 is commonly preferred for flexibility. Always return 404 Not Found if the code does not exist or has expired. Include appropriate cache-control headers when you want proxies to respect your choice. A frequent misconception is thinking redirect type only affects SEO; it also defines caching and client behavior. Choose based on whether mappings remain stable and whether each hit should be visible to your analytics pipeline. Redirecting — GET /{shortCode} means 302 is flexible and analytics-friendly; 301 caches and is permanent. choose based on changeability and performance needs.. In practical terms, redirect responses, caching, and analytics trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A Pastebin create flow is another create operation: POST /api/v1/pastes. The request must include content and may include optional fields such as syntaxHighlightingLanguage, expirationOption, accessControl, and a password for private pastes. The server validates content length and required fields and derives expirationDate from the chosen expirationOption. On success return 201 Created with pasteUrl and pasteId plus metadata like createdAt and expirationDate. If required fields are missing return 400 Bad Request with clear details, and if a password is required but not supplied return a 400 error describing the issue. For private pastes, the retrieve flow should require an authorization or a separate unlock step that accepts a password. One misconception is returning full error stacks or internal debugging information in error bodies — avoid exposing internals. Design responses so clients can render a link immediately and know when a paste expires. This contract supports features like unlisted vs public pastes and lays the groundwork for access checks during retrieval. Pastebin — POST /api/v1/pastes means post /api/v1/pastes includes required content plus optional fields for language, expiration, and access control.. In practical terms, creating pastes with syntax, expiry, and access control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Retrieval has two patterns for a Pastebin: direct GET for public/unlisted pastes and a separate unlock step for password-protected ones. For public pastes a GET /api/v1/pastes/{pasteId} returns 200 OK with the paste content and metadata. If the paste is not found or expired return 404 Not Found. For private pastes, require the client to authenticate or to POST a password to /api/v1/pastes/{pasteId}/unlock. On successful unlock return the paste content and an otherwise appropriate 200 OK. If the password is missing or incorrect return 403 Forbidden to indicate an authorization problem. Design the unlock endpoint to avoid leaking information; for instance, do not reveal whether a paste exists in error messages. A common mistake is using the same response code for missing paste and wrong password; instead use 404 for non-existent, 403 for authorization failure. Also plan for authorization headers or A P I tokens for user-scoped pastes. This clear separation of retrieval and unlocking keeps public reads fast while isolating authentication checks to a narrower flow. Paste Retrieve — GET and Unlock means use get for public retrieval and a dedicated unlock endpoint for private, password-protected pastes to keep flows explicit.. In practical terms, retrieving public pastes and unlocking private ones. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Choosing between 301 and 302 affects more than SEO: it controls client and proxy caching. A 301 Moved Permanently is often cached by browsers and intermediaries, which can bypass your redirect service on subsequent requests. That helps performance but makes changing the target URL difficult because clients may never re-query the shortener. A 302 Found or 307 Temporary Redirect avoids that caching behavior so every click hits your service. That is useful when you want to gather analytics on each click, perform per-request logic, or update mappings. If you need analytics, URL editing, or A/B testing, prefer 302. If mapping is truly permanent and you want to offload traffic from your servers, 301 is acceptable. Remember to include Cache-Control headers when you need finer control. Idempotence is crucial for resilient APIs because network clients may retry requests automatically. An idempotent operation produces the same result whether it is applied once or multiple times. In HTTP, GET, PUT, and DELETE are expected to be idempotent; POST is not. For example, deleting a resource twice with DELETE yields the same final state as deleting it once. Creating a new resource with POST typically creates duplicates if retried, which can be problematic. To handle this, APIs can accept idempotency keys supplied by clients; the server stores the key and ensures the operation only executes once for that key. Alternatively, use deterministic PUT on a resource path derived from a client-provided id so repeated calls replace the same resource. A misconception is thinking that POST cannot ever be safe to retry — with an idempotency key or a unique client-generated identifier, POST can be made effectively idempotent. Always document which operations are safe to retry, and consider returning idempotency results and guidance in error messages so clients can react appropriately. This checklist captures practical mistakes I see often and the corrective design choices to prevent them. First, avoid using inappropriate HTTP methods — creation should use POST, retrieval GET, updates PUT/PATCH, and deletion DELETE. Second, return clear error responses with appropriate status codes like 400 for validation errors, 403 for authorization failures, 404 for missing resources, and 500 only for server faults.
